title: Variables, print() and f-strings
summary: A variable is a name for a value. print() shows values, and f-strings drop them into text.

basics.heading: A name for a value
basics.body: Use a single = to store a value under a name. Assigning again replaces the old value: a variable holds one value at a time, and each line uses the value from the line before.
basics.code:
cells = 120
cells = cells + 30
print(cells)

basics.heading: Good names
basics.body: Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit or contain spaces or hyphens. They are case-sensitive: Gene and gene are different names.

basics.heading: print() and f-strings
basics.body: print() shows each item it is given, separated by a space. An f-string — text with an f in front — replaces every {name} with that variable's value. Without the f, the braces are printed as they are.
basics.code:
gene = "TP53"
length = 393
print("Gene:", gene)
print(f"{gene} has {length} amino acids")
print("{gene} has {length} amino acids")
basics.output:
Gene: TP53
TP53 has 393 amino acids
{gene} has {length} amino acids

further.heading: Formatting numbers
further.body: Inside the braces you can put a whole expression, and after a colon a format: :.2f shows two decimal places, :.0f none.
further.code:
ratio = 2 / 3
print(f"{ratio:.2f}")
print(f"{ratio * 100:.0f} percent")

further.heading: Copying a value, not a link
further.body: b = a copies the value a has at that moment. Changing a afterwards does not change b. Shortcuts such as += update a variable using its own value.
further.code:
a = 3
b = a
a += 1
print(a, b)

title: Data types and converting between them
summary: Every value has a type — int, float, str or bool — and the type decides what you can do with it.

basics.heading: The four types
basics.body: Whole numbers are int, numbers with a decimal point are float, anything in quotes is a str (string), and True/False are bool. type() tells you which one you have.
basics.code:
print(type(42))
print(type(3.0))
print(type("42"))
print(type(True))

basics.heading: Quotes change everything
basics.body: With strings, + joins and * repeats; with numbers they add and multiply. Text read from a file is always a string, so convert it before doing maths.
basics.code:
print("12" + "3")
print(int("12") + 3)
print(str(4) + " wells")

further.heading: Conversions have rules
further.body: int() on a float cuts off the decimal part — it does not round. int() cannot read text with a decimal point (ValueError): go through float() first. Division with / always gives a float.
further.code:
print(int(7.9))
print(int(float("3.5")))
print(10 / 2)

title: Operators: arithmetic, comparison and logic
summary: Operators do the maths, compare values, and combine True/False answers.

basics.heading: Arithmetic
basics.body: ** is a power, // divides and drops the decimal part, % gives the remainder. Python follows the usual order — ** first, then * / // %, then + and - — and brackets go first of all.

basics.heading: Comparisons and logic
basics.body: == asks 'equal?' (a single = stores a value). != means 'not equal'. and needs both sides True, or needs at least one, and not flips True and False.
basics.code:
od = 0.45
print(od == 0.45, od != 0.45)
print(od > 0.4 and od < 0.6)
print(not od > 0.4)

further.heading: Chained comparisons and splitting units
further.body: 0.4 < od < 0.6 means 0.4 < od and od < 0.6. Together, // and % split a quantity into whole units and what is left over.
further.code:
od = 0.7
print(0.4 < od < 0.6)
seconds = 200
print(seconds // 60, "min", seconds % 60, "s")

title: Lists
summary: A list holds many values in order. You can index it, slice it and change it.

basics.heading: Indexing and slicing
basics.body: Counting starts at 0; -1 is the last item. A slice [start:stop] stops before stop, and leaving a side out runs to that end.
basics.code:
weights = [21, 19, 25, 23]
print(weights[0], weights[-1])
print(weights[1:3], weights[:2])

basics.heading: Changing a list
basics.body: .append() adds to the end, .insert() at a position, and x[i] = value replaces an item. len(), sum(), min() and max() summarise a list of numbers.
basics.code:
weights = [21, 19, 25]
weights.append(23)
weights[0] = 22
print(weights, len(weights), sum(weights) / len(weights))

further.heading: Two names, one list
further.body: b = a does not copy a list: both names point to the same list, so a change through one shows up in the other. .copy() makes an independent list.
further.code:
a = [3, 1, 2]
b = a
c = a.copy()
a.append(9)
print(b, c)

further.heading: sort() versus sorted()
further.body: .sort() reorders the list itself and returns None. sorted() gives back a new sorted list and leaves the original alone.
further.code:
x = [5, 2, 8]
y = sorted(x)
print(x, y)
print(x.sort(), x)

further.heading: Lists inside lists
further.body: Each item can itself be a list. Index twice: first the row, then the item in it.
further.code:
plate = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(plate[1], plate[1][2])

title: Strings
summary: A string is a sequence of characters — indexed and sliced like a list, with its own methods.

basics.heading: A sequence of characters
basics.body: len(), indexing and slicing work just as they do for lists. in checks whether one piece of text appears inside another.
basics.code:
dna = "GATTACA"
print(len(dna), dna[0], dna[2:5], dna[-2:])
print("TTA" in dna)

basics.heading: Methods return a new string
basics.body: Strings cannot be changed in place. .upper(), .replace() and friends hand back a new string — store it, or it is lost.
basics.code:
dna = "atgc"
dna.upper()
print(dna)
dna = dna.upper()
print(dna, dna.replace("T", "U"))

basics.heading: Useful methods
basics.body: .count() counts a piece of text, .find() gives where it starts, .split() cuts text into a list and .strip() removes spaces and newlines at both ends.
basics.code:
line = "  sample_07,GATTACA \n"
clean = line.strip()
print(clean.split(","))
print(clean.count("A"), clean.find("GAT"))

further.heading: Reversing, joining and searching
further.body: A step of -1 reverses. "-".join(list) glues strings together with a separator. .find() returns -1 when the text is not there, and .count() does not count overlapping matches.
further.code:
print("ACGT"[::-1])
print("-".join(["ATG", "GCC", "TAA"]))
print("ATGC".find("X"), "AAAA".count("AA"))

title: Dictionaries
summary: A dictionary is a lookup table: each key points to a value.

basics.heading: Looking things up
basics.body: Square brackets with a key give its value; assigning to a new key adds it. Reading a key that is not there raises a KeyError — keys are case-sensitive.

basics.heading: .get() for missing keys
basics.body: .get(key, default) returns the default instead of raising an error. That makes it the standard way to count.

basics.heading: Looping through a dictionary
basics.body: .items() gives each key together with its value; .keys() and .values() give one side.

further.heading: Building and sorting
further.body: zip() pairs two lists, and dict() turns the pairs into a dictionary. sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]) sorts the pairs by value; add reverse=True for largest first.
further.code:
d = dict(zip(["rat", "bat", "cat"], [3, 7, 5]))
ranked = sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)
print(ranked[0])

further.heading: Comprehensions and nesting
further.body: A dictionary comprehension builds key: value pairs in one line. A value can itself be a dictionary — look up twice.

title: for loops and range()
summary: A for loop runs the same lines once for every item.

basics.heading: Once per item
basics.body: The indented lines run once for each item, with the loop variable set to that item. Two patterns come up again and again: a running total that starts at 0, and a new list that starts empty.
basics.code:
total = 0
doubled = []
for v in [2, 3, 5]:
    total += v
    doubled.append(v * 2)
print(total, doubled)

basics.heading: range()
basics.body: range(stop) counts from 0 up to — not including — stop. range(start, stop, step) changes where it starts and how far it jumps.
basics.code:
print(list(range(4)))
print(list(range(2, 6)))
print(list(range(0, 10, 3)))

basics.heading: break
basics.body: break leaves the loop straight away; the loop variable keeps its last value.

further.heading: enumerate() and zip()
further.body: enumerate() gives each position together with its item. zip() walks two lists side by side.

further.heading: List comprehensions
further.body: [expression for item in list] builds a new list in one line.
further.code: print([x * x for x in range(5)])

further.heading: while loops
further.body: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is True — use it when you do not know in advance how many runs you need.
further.code:
n = 1
steps = 0
while n < 100:
    n = n * 3
    steps += 1
print(n, steps)

title: if, elif and else
summary: if statements let a program make decisions.

slides.title: Two Ways to Go — if / else

basics.heading: One chain, one branch
basics.body: Python checks the conditions from the top and runs the first branch that is True; the rest of the chain is skipped. else takes no condition. Indentation decides which lines belong to each branch.

basics.heading: Decisions inside a loop
basics.body: Combine a loop with an if to count or collect only the items that pass a test.

basics.heading: Separate ifs are not a chain
basics.body: Two separate if statements are each checked, so both can run. Use elif when only one branch should.

further.heading: Conditional expressions
further.body: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false picks one of two values in a single line.
further.code:
x = 7
print("even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd")

further.heading: Filtering with comprehensions
further.body: An if at the end of a comprehension keeps only the items that pass; an if/else at the front labels every item. not in checks that something is absent.
further.code:
values = [3, 8, 1, 9]
print([v for v in values if v > 2])
print(["H" if v > 5 else "L" for v in values])
print([b for b in "ANTG" if b not in "N"])

title: Functions
summary: A function packages a few lines under a name, so you can run them again with different inputs.

slides.title: Give It Something to Work On

basics.heading: def, parameters and return
basics.body: def starts a function. The names in brackets are parameters; the values you pass in the call are arguments. return hands a result back to the caller and ends the function.

basics.heading: print is not return
basics.body: A function without return hands back None. Printing inside a function shows a value, but the caller cannot use it.
basics.code:
def shout(x):
    print(x.upper())

result = shout("hi")
print(result)

basics.heading: Defaults and named arguments
basics.body: A default value is used when the argument is left out. Arguments can also be passed by name, in any order.

further.heading: Returning several values
further.body: return a, b hands back a tuple; unpack it straight into two names.

further.heading: Local variables
further.body: Variables created inside a function are local: they disappear when it ends and never change a variable with the same name outside.
further.code:
x = 5

def change():
    x = 99
    return x

print(change(), x)

further.heading: Docstrings
further.body: A string on the first line of a function documents it; Python stores it as __doc__, and help() shows it.
further.code:
def count_cells(image):
    """Count the cells in an image."""
    return 0

print(count_cells.__doc__)
further.output: Count the cells in an image.

title: Errors and how to handle them
summary: Errors are normal. Reading the error name tells you what went wrong; try/except lets a program carry on.

basics.heading: The common errors
basics.body: NameError — a name that was never created. TypeError — the wrong type, e.g. "A" + 1. ValueError — the right type but an impossible value, e.g. int("abc"). IndexError — a position past the end. KeyError — a dictionary key that is not there. The last line of the error message names it.

basics.heading: Check first, or try
basics.body: An if guard checks before something can go wrong. try/except runs the risky line and, if that error happens, runs the except block instead of crashing.

basics.heading: raise
basics.body: raise stops a function with an error of your choosing — better than carrying on with bad data. The caller can catch it.

further.heading: else and finally
further.body: else runs only when the try block raised nothing; finally runs every time, error or not.
further.output:
7 doubled is 14
checked 7
x is not a number
checked x

further.heading: Errors travel up
further.body: An error inside a function travels back to whoever called it, where an except can catch it. With several except blocks, the first matching one runs.
